🇷🇺🇺🇦🇺🇸🇰🇿🛢 Novorossiysk, There Air Defense, U.S. Worries On Oil Profits:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukrainian anti-ship missiles, jet-powered aerial drones and sea drones blitzed a major Russian naval base on the Black Sea coast in a “unique” nighttime operation, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Wednesday.
Cutting-edge drones developed by Kyiv since Russia invaded more than four years ago have repeatedly targeted Russian ships in the Black Sea, including warships and oil tankers. Both countries have Black Sea shorelines.
Ukraine’s uncrewed fleet has succeeded in limiting the movements of Russia’s once-dominant Black Sea navy, Kyiv officials say, in one of the country’s biggest feats of the war.
But Ukrainian officials reckon that Russian President Vladimir Putin is bent on prosecuting the invasion, despite his bigger army’s slow and costly progress on the battlefield and U.S. diplomatic efforts to find a settlement.
Putin is planning “an additional rapid mobilization of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year,” Zelenskyy said on social media late Tuesday, citing Ukrainian intel.
Those reports have also said recently that Russia is expanding production of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, both of which are hard for Ukrainian air defenses to counter.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is also trying to scale up its weapons manufacturing through agreements with partner countries, as both countries apparently plan to fight on.
The Ukrainian military “carried out a unique operation targeting the naval base in Novorossiysk — the last major stronghold of the Russian fleet in the Black Sea,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
The attack struck air defenses, piers and other port infrastructure in the Krasnodar region city, he added.
Krasnodar region Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said that hundreds of Ukrainian drones attacked Novorossiysk, Anapa and Gelendzhik and the Temryuk district overnight.
Novorossiysk is also home to a key international oil terminal. The Grushovaya oil transshipment complex near Novorossiysk is one of the largest transshipment hubs in southern Russia for oil and petroleum products.
Last Feb, the U.S. State Department expressed its displeasure about Ukraine’s attacks on Novorossiysk, saying they have impacted U.S. oil interests in ⁠Kazakhstan.
The Caspian Pipeline Consortium operates a pipeline from the Caspian coast in northwest Kazakhstan to Novorossiysk. The pipeline handles much of the crude exports from three major Kazakh fields in which major U.S. energy companies, Chevron and ExxonMobil, have stakes.
In illegally annexed Crimea, air defenses downed 115 Ukrainian drones over Sevastopol overnight, the city’s Russia-appointed head said, adding that 10 apartment buildings and 25 private houses were damaged.
Russian air defenses downed more than 500 Ukrainian drones Moscow said.
In Novorossiysk, an eight-year old child was killed in the attack, and a person wounded when his house in the Temryuk region was hit later died in hospital, Kondratyev said. He added that 12 other people in the region were wounded.
Debris from downed drones fell on the territory of four industrial plants and 21 residential buildings, according to Kondratyev, but officials gave no details of any damage.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force said Wednesday that Russia fired 138 long-range strike drones as well as an unspecified number of missiles at Ukraine during the night. Damage was recorded at 16 locations across the country, it said.
In the southern Kherson region of Ukraine, a large-scale Russian drone attack overnight killed two people and wounded two others, regional head Oleksandr Prokudin said Wednesday.
The attacks also destroyed a shopping mall in the southern Ukraine city of Zaporizhzhia.
---
However, U.S. leadership is pushing back, specifically Vance and Trump, as they are concerned about American companies' financial connections to Russia and Kazakhstan's oil trade. More in next post.

⚡️⚡🇾🇪 BREAKING — Yemen is witnessing its largest escalation in ground fighting since the 2022 truce, with Houthi forces opening or intensifying operations across multiple fronts as fighting spreads from Marib to the Red Sea coast.
Heavy clashes are currently being reported around Mokha and Hays in western Yemen, where Houthi forces are attempting to advance south along the Red Sea coastal axis against Saudi-backed government forces. Pro-Houthi and battlefield mapping sources report new territorial advances along the road south of Hays and northeast of Mawza, potentially threatening approaches toward the strategically important port of Mokha.
The fighting follows several days of escalating Houthi missile and drone attacks against Mokha and its port, alongside renewed combat around Marib, where Houthi forces have also increased military pressure against government-held positions.
The simultaneous escalation is particularly significant because Mokha sits close to the Bab al-Mandab maritime chokepoint, while Marib remains one of the most strategically important government-held areas in northern Yemen.
Reports from battlefield sources now claim Houthi forces are massing around Marib and that a larger offensive could follow.
The renewed fighting increasingly threatens to unravel the relative calm that had largely frozen Yemen's major frontlines since 2022.

Lockheed Martin blurs the line between civilian and military, turning 5G into future battlespace
The Pentagon military contractor has demonstrated an AI-powered drone-tracking system that uses existing commercial telecommunications infrastructure instead of a separate detection network.
What's known about the system?
🔴 Lockheed Martin's NetSense Airspace Awareness-as-a-Service platform uses the existing 5G network to detect changes in radio signals caused by drones. AI then analyzes those changes to spot, identify, track and predict the movement of unmanned aerial vehicles
🔴 The key advantage is scale: because 5G infrastructure already exists across cities, the system could potentially monitor large areas without building a separate network of sensors
🔴 Lockheed Martin says the tool could be used to secure critical civilian infrastructure, including power plants, schools, hospitals and airports. Astris AI, a Lockheed Martin subsidiary, will offer NetSense via a subscription-based model, with pilot deployments planned for late 2026 and early 2027.
🤔 What could go wrong?
🌏 While the platform’s advocates point to the growing threat posed by unauthorized drones, critics are increasingly concerned about military contractor Lockheed Martin becoming more deeply embedded in civilian life and using civilian infrastructure for military and intelligence purposes. Bringing military-grade tracking technology into neighborhoods, schools and hospitals raises concerns about the “militarization” of everyday life
🌏 NetSense continuously monitors changes in radio signals across urban areas, raising concerns that its “always-on” sensing could potentially be used to track not only drones in the air, but also vehicles on the ground — and, depending on how the system is deployed, potentially people without their knowledge
🌏 Lockheed Martin’s drone-tracking system is not immune to errors or hacking, with false alarms and public panic among the least serious potential consequences
🌏 By integrating sensitive security data into commercial cellular networks, NetSense could effectively turn civilian telecom infrastructure into a target — and potentially a new digital battleground for attackers. In other words, the more security functions are layered onto civilian networks, the greater the potential consequences if those networks are compromised.
More importantly, NetSense is part of Lockheed Martin’s broader 5G MIL program, which integrates commercial 5G with military networks through tactical gateways and open architecture. The goal? “Battlespace dominance,” according to the program’s own website.
📑 Main pillars of 5G MIL program:
➡️ Network cohesion: "In the 21st Century battlespace, dominance will be determined by the ability to bring together high-tech platforms into one cohesive network that spans every domain – air, land, sea, space and cyber"
➡️ Resilient communications: Combines military and commercial 5G infrastructure to maintain communications in contested environments
➡️ Existing networks: Integrates legacy tactical networks through distributed gateways, reducing single points of failure
➡️ Combating threats: AI, edge computing and 5G MIL connectivity allow to connect all assets seamlessly "in the joint battlespace for unparalleled situational awareness to enable decisive action".
